You Probably Are, Too.   Plus, what does fund “redemption” mean?     Emil Nolde, "Dance Around the Golden Calf" (1910), Pinakothek der Moderne, Munich WIKIMEDIA COMMONS   Fellow investors,

   In July 2015, I called gold a “ pet rock ” when it was below $1,150 an ounce. Five years later, it had gained almost 70% — at which point I was skeptical again . Naturally, over the next five years, gold nearly doubled.

   But I’m not the only one who’s always wrong about gold.

   Gold bugs love to proclaim that their favorite metal is a hedge against inflation. Let’s see. Here’s inflation from late 2020 to mid 2022:

         And here’s gold over the same period:

         Inflation soared, gold went down. Inconvenient!

   Never mind that, say the gold bugs. It’s also a hedge against geopolitical turmoil.

   Well, here’s how gold has done since the day before the war in Iran began:

         Umm, never mind that, gold bugs say. Gold has to go up, because central banks around the world will keep buying more of it.

   In the third quarter, central banks bought the greatest quantity of gold since late 2024 , and their year-to-date purchases are up 6% from the same period last year.

   The price of gold is down about 5% year-to-date.

   The upshot: As soon as one of their rationales for buying gold gets refuted in the market, gold bugs skitter around until they find a new one, without even bothering to admit they were wrong about the last one.

   For some people, owning gold is a part of their identity, almost an article of religious belief. No matter what the evidence says or how it changes, their faith never wavers.

   Other types of investors also change their reasoning without ever changing their mind . Think how bitcoin was supposed to replace dollars as an everyday currency, then became an “uncorrelated asset,” then a “store of value.” Now one of the main arguments seems to be that it’s a scarce collectible.

   Let me be clear about gold. It is a decent store of value over extremely long periods; its purchasing power has held more or less steady since ancient Roman times . Owning a bit of it (or shares of gold-mining companies when they’re cheap) isn’t the worst idea in the world. But constantly changing your mind about why it has to become more valuable, without ever questioning whether it has to become more valuable, is like standing on your head and complaining that the world is upside down.

   This is an edition of the Intelligent Investor newsletter, where Jason Zweig writes twice monthly about investment strategy and how to think about money. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here . 

       Wall Street Words: “Redemption”   The great Austrian writer Karl Kraus had a saying I like: “The closer one looks at a word, the farther away it moves.” In the vocabulary of investing, redemption behaves like that. To request a redemption, as so many investors in private-credit funds have been doing lately , is to ask to get your money out of a fund by selling your shares, usually back to the fund’s sponsor. Why does the word for that sound as if you’re seeking eternal salvation for your soul?

   Redemption is rooted in the Latin redimere, which meant to buy back or recover by purchase, to ransom a prisoner or slave, or to buy someone off as a way to escape obligation or punishment. “Redeem” was commonly used in the 15th and 16th centuries to describe such transactions.

   This translation of Cicero’s “On Old Age,” published by William Caxton in 1481, narrates how the Roman statesman Marcus Atilius was released from prison in Carthage on his promise to “redeme” Carthaginians held captive in Rome:

     William Caxton (1481) UNIVERSITY OF IOWA LIBRARIES   …[they] entreated him and desired that he should for his deliverance out of prison make to be redeemed, delivered and recovered many of their young lords, knights and [gentlemen] of Carthage taken prisoners before-times amongst the Romans…. 

   At the same time, redemption (to be “redemyd”) was used in the religious sense to mean deliverance from sin or rescue from hell:

     William Caxton, "The Golden Legend" (1483) UNIVERSITY OF MICHIGAN   …And his blessed son which in human nature had redeemed and saved the world…. 

   In the 14th to 16th centuries, a synonym for “to redeem” was “to again-buy,” often spelled agen-bye — a direct echo of the Latin redimere, to buy again.

   Investors fleeing private-credit and other alternative funds might well feel as if redeeming their shares is the equivalent of redeeming themselves from captivity or punishment—especially if they have an urgent need for cash before even the best of these funds can deliver their potential for higher returns. Before you buy, make sure you won’t have to again-buy.

   This is the latest in a series on the origin and history of financial words. You can read the earlier installments here: 

   • bond 

   • hedge fund 

   • fund 

   • credit 

   • volatile 

   • realize 

   • mania 

   • money 

   • stock 

   • cash 

   • inflation 

       “Our Survey Said!”   My eyebrows went up recently when I got a press release from the American Investment Council, a trade association for the private-equity industry.

   “Most physicians working in private equity-backed practices reported improvements in patient access, the addition of new practices or expanded medical services, and operational capacity,” said the release. “In every category surveyed, physicians reported more favorable outcomes, for their practices and patients, following private equity investment.”

   Another release stated that two-thirds to more than three-quarters of PE-backed physicians reported improved patient access, positive or no impact on interactions with patients, and expanded-care options.

   That seemed high. A survey published in the American Medical Association’s JAMA Internal Medicine journal in March 2024 , with 525 respondents, found drastically different results. Half reported that private-equity ownership was “worse or much worse” than either not-for-profit or independent ownership; more than half said it was bad for “physician well-being” and the cost of healthcare.

   Only 11% of these doctors viewed PE ownership as being “positive or somewhat positive.”

   Hmmm.

   When I clicked through to the survey report that the American Investment Council was citing, I found this:

     "Private Equity and Healthcare Delivery," p. 6 HEALTHMANAGEMENT.COM   You read that right. At least two-thirds of 30 doctors working in private-equity-backed settings view private-equity ownership at least somewhat positively! Hey, that could be, like, 21 or 22 people! Maybe even more!

   The U.S. has approximately 1 million active physicians.

   To be fair, this survey didn’t claim to be a representative sample of all U.S. doctors. It’s a pretty representative sample of private-equity propaganda, though.

       Catching Up   Here are my latest columns.

   On sector funds that seek to deliver undiluted exposure to the biggest stocks within industries: The Extra-Strength Funds That Are Too Much of a Good Thing . These funds could be useful to traders, but investors should approach them with caution.

   On how to think about the stock market’s plunge the day after the midterm elections: How to Keep These Wild Market Moves From Hijacking Your Financial Future . Instead of letting your emotions sway your decisions, be sure you have rules in place that can make your decisions for you.

I’m Always Wrong About Gold. You Probably Are, Too.
 
Plus, what does fund “redemption” mean?
 
 
Emil Nolde, "Dance Around the Golden Calf" (1910), Pinakothek der Moderne, Munich WIKIMEDIA COMMONS
 

Fellow investors,

 

In July 2015, I called gold a “pet rock” when it was below $1,150 an ounce. Five years later, it had gained almost 70% — at which point I was skeptical again. Naturally, over the next five years, gold nearly doubled.

 

But I’m not the only one who’s always wrong about gold.

 

Gold bugs love to proclaim that their favorite metal is a hedge against inflation. Let’s see. Here’s inflation from late 2020 to mid 2022:

 
 
 
 

And here’s gold over the same period:

 
 
 
 

Inflation soared, gold went down. Inconvenient!

 

Never mind that, say the gold bugs. It’s also a hedge against geopolitical turmoil.

 

Well, here’s how gold has done since the day before the war in Iran began:

 
 
 
 

Umm, never mind that, gold bugs say. Gold has to go up, because central banks around the world will keep buying more of it.

 

In the third quarter, central banks bought the greatest quantity of gold since late 2024, and their year-to-date purchases are up 6% from the same period last year.

 

The price of gold is down about 5% year-to-date.

 

The upshot: As soon as one of their rationales for buying gold gets refuted in the market, gold bugs skitter around until they find a new one, without even bothering to admit they were wrong about the last one.

 

For some people, owning gold is a part of their identity, almost an article of religious belief. No matter what the evidence says or how it changes, their faith never wavers.

 

Other types of investors also change their reasoning without ever changing their mind. Think how bitcoin was supposed to replace dollars as an everyday currency, then became an “uncorrelated asset,” then a “store of value.” Now one of the main arguments seems to be that it’s a scarce collectible.

 

Let me be clear about gold. It is a decent store of value over extremely long periods; its purchasing power has held more or less steady since ancient Roman times. Owning a bit of it (or shares of gold-mining companies when they’re cheap) isn’t the worst idea in the world. But constantly changing your mind about why it has to become more valuable, without ever questioning whether it has to become more valuable, is like standing on your head and complaining that the world is upside down.

 

This is an edition of the Intelligent Investor newsletter, where Jason Zweig writes twice monthly about investment strategy and how to think about money. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

Wall Street Words: “Redemption”

 

The great Austrian writer Karl Kraus had a saying I like: “The closer one looks at a word, the farther away it moves.” In the vocabulary of investing, redemption behaves like that. To request a redemption, as so many investors in private-credit funds have been doing lately, is to ask to get your money out of a fund by selling your shares, usually back to the fund’s sponsor. Why does the word for that sound as if you’re seeking eternal salvation for your soul?

 

Redemption is rooted in the Latin redimere, which meant to buy back or recover by purchase, to ransom a prisoner or slave, or to buy someone off as a way to escape obligation or punishment. “Redeem” was commonly used in the 15th and 16th centuries to describe such transactions.

 

This translation of Cicero’s “On Old Age,” published by William Caxton in 1481, narrates how the Roman statesman Marcus Atilius was released from prison in Carthage on his promise to “redeme” Carthaginians held captive in Rome:

 
 
William Caxton (1481) UNIVERSITY OF IOWA LIBRARIES
 

…[they] entreated him and desired that he should for his deliverance out of prison make to be redeemed, delivered and recovered many of their young lords, knights and [gentlemen] of Carthage taken prisoners before-times amongst the Romans….

 

At the same time, redemption (to be “redemyd”) was used in the religious sense to mean deliverance from sin or rescue from hell:

 
 
William Caxton, "The Golden Legend" (1483) UNIVERSITY OF MICHIGAN
 

…And his blessed son which in human nature had redeemed and saved the world….

 

In the 14th to 16th centuries, a synonym for “to redeem” was “to again-buy,” often spelled agen-bye — a direct echo of the Latin redimere, to buy again.

 

Investors fleeing private-credit and other alternative funds might well feel as if redeeming their shares is the equivalent of redeeming themselves from captivity or punishment—especially if they have an urgent need for cash before even the best of these funds can deliver their potential for higher returns. Before you buy, make sure you won’t have to again-buy.

 

This is the latest in a series on the origin and history of financial words. You can read the earlier installments here:

 

• bond

 

• hedge fund

 

• fund

 

• credit

 

• volatile

 

• realize

 

• mania

 

• money

 

• stock

 

• cash

 

• inflation

 
 
 

“Our Survey Said!”

 

My eyebrows went up recently when I got a press release from the American Investment Council, a trade association for the private-equity industry.

 

“Most physicians working in private equity-backed practices reported improvements in patient access, the addition of new practices or expanded medical services, and operational capacity,” said the release. “In every category surveyed, physicians reported more favorable outcomes, for their practices and patients, following private equity investment.”

 

Another release stated that two-thirds to more than three-quarters of PE-backed physicians reported improved patient access, positive or no impact on interactions with patients, and expanded-care options.

 

That seemed high. A survey published in the American Medical Association’s JAMA Internal Medicine journal in March 2024, with 525 respondents, found drastically different results. Half reported that private-equity ownership was “worse or much worse” than either not-for-profit or independent ownership; more than half said it was bad for “physician well-being” and the cost of healthcare.

 

Only 11% of these doctors viewed PE ownership as being “positive or somewhat positive.”

 

Hmmm.

 

When I clicked through to the survey report that the American Investment Council was citing, I found this:

 
 
"Private Equity and Healthcare Delivery," p. 6 HEALTHMANAGEMENT.COM
 

You read that right. At least two-thirds of 30 doctors working in private-equity-backed settings view private-equity ownership at least somewhat positively! Hey, that could be, like, 21 or 22 people! Maybe even more!

 

The U.S. has approximately 1 million active physicians.

 

To be fair, this survey didn’t claim to be a representative sample of all U.S. doctors. It’s a pretty representative sample of private-equity propaganda, though.
